results.result: Mice fed Western diet (WD) or ketogenic diet (KD) for 2 weeks showed significantly enhanced hypothermia starting at 10 hr post-LPS injection and 100% mortality by 26 hr, compared to 100% survival in standard chow (SC)-fed mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are directly supported by experimental data in Figure 1A-B showing temperature loss and survival curves. The data clearly demonstrate diet-dependent differences in endotoxemia severity and mortality with appropriate statistical comparisons.

results.result: Hypoglycemia was not a driver of enhanced disease severity in WD- and KD-fed mice, as all diet groups displayed similar levels of LPS-induced hypoglycemia during disease.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7 are supported by blood glucose measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) showing no significant differences between diet groups during LPS challenge. This appropriately rules out hypoglycemia as a confounding variable.

results.result: At 5 hr post-LPS injection, WD- and KD-fed mice showed significantly higher expression of inflammatory cytokines (Tnf, Il6, and Il1b for WD; Tnf and Il6 for KD) compared to SC-fed mice, indicating diets enriched in SFAs are associated with hyper-inflammatory responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C13 are supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1C-E showing elevated cytokine expression. The statistical analyses appear appropriate with multiple timepoints measured. The conclusion about SFA-enriched diets is reasonably inferred from the data.

results.result: WD- and KD-fed mice showed increased Il10 expression and elevated Il10:Tnf ratios at later timepoints (10-20 hr), indicating an enhanced immunoparalytic phenotype that correlates with disease severity, similar to clinical sepsis.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C19 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 1F-G) and appropriate clinical citations. The temporal pattern of early hyper-inflammation followed by immunoparalysis is well-documented. However, the mechanistic link between the ratio and mortality could be strengthened.

results.result: The KD-associated increase in endotoxemia severity and mortality is independent of diet-associated microbiome, as demonstrated in germ-free mice showing similar phenotypes to conventional mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C25 are supported by experiments in germ-free mice (Figure 1H-I) showing similar disease outcomes as conventional mice. This is a critical control demonstrating microbiome-independent effects. The experimental design appropriately addresses this confounding variable.

results.result: WD- and KD-fed germ-free mice displayed enhanced expression of inflammatory cytokines (Tnf, Il1b at 5-10 hr; Il6 at 5 hr) compared to SC-fed germ-free mice following LPS challenge.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C31 are supported by qRT-PCR data from germ-free mice (Figure 1J-L). The data confirm that early hyper-inflammatory responses occur independent of microbiome, strengthening the conclusion that dietary SFAs directly affect immune responses.

results.result: The late immunoparalytic phenotype (elevated Il10:Tnf ratio) observed in conventional SFA-fed mice was absent in germ-free mice, suggesting this response is microbiome-dependent, while early hyper-inflammation is microbiome-independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by comparing conventional (Figure 1F-G) and germ-free (Figure 1M-N) mouse data. This differential microbiome dependence is a novel finding that distinguishes two phases of the immune response. The inference is logical and well-supported.

results.result: KD feeding for 2 weeks significantly enhanced hematopoietic stem cell populations (ST-HSCs, LT-HSCs, and MPPs) in wild-type mice, while WD feeding showed no significant changes, demonstrating that SFA-enriched diets can alter hematopoiesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 are supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 2C) with appropriate statistical comparisons. This is the first demonstration that KD alone (without genetic predisposition like Ldlr-/-) can alter HSC compartments. The finding is novel and well-controlled.

results.result: Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) from WD- and KD-fed mice, cultured ex vivo for 7 days, showed significantly enhanced TNF secretion upon LPS stimulation, with KD-derived BMDMs also showing enhanced IL-6, indicating long-lasting inflammatory reprogramming in the bone marrow.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 are supported by ELISA data (Figure 2D-E) from BMDMs cultured for 7 days after isolation. The 7-day culture period is critical for demonstrating persistent reprogramming rather than acute priming. This provides strong evidence for trained immunity.

results.result: Bone marrow monocytes and splenocytes from KD-fed mice showed enhanced inflammatory responses to LPS ex vivo without baseline inflammation, demonstrating that KD induces trained immunity characterized by normal homeostatic state but hyper-responsiveness to secondary challenge.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C57 are supported by qRT-PCR data from BMMs and splenocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-F). The distinction between homeostatic and challenged states is important for defining trained immunity versus priming. The data support this distinction.

results.result: Two weeks of KD feeding significantly altered circulating lipid profiles, with increased free palmitic acid (PA; C16:0) and PA-containing lipids (TAGs and PCs) in serum compared to SC-fed mice, as demonstrated by lipidomics analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 are supported by LC-MS/MS lipidomics data (Figure 3A-D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D) showing distinct lipid profiles with PCA analysis demonstrating clear separation between diet groups. The identification of PA as a key altered lipid is well-supported.

results.result: Pre-treatment of BMDMs with physiologically relevant concentrations of PA (0.5-1 mM) for 12-24 hr induced a hyper-inflammatory response to secondary LPS challenge, with enhanced expression and secretion of TNF, IL-6, and IL-1β, independent of significant cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C80 are supported by qRT-PCR and ELISA data (Figure 3E-J, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) with appropriate controls including cell death assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). The dose-response and time-course experiments strengthen the conclusions. The PA concentrations used are physiologically relevant.

results.result: Inhibition of ceramide synthesis with Fumonisin B1 (FB1) significantly reduced PA-induced hyper-inflammatory responses in BMDMs, demonstrating that ceramide synthesis is required for PA-mediated trained immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86 are supported by ELISA data (Figure 3K-M) showing that FB1 co-treatment blocks PA-induced cytokine secretion. This mechanistic experiment is critical for establishing the ceramide pathway as the mediator of PA effects. The inference is well-supported.

results.result: Systemic PA injection (750 mM ethyl palmitate i.p.) for 12 hr, but not shorter durations, was sufficient to enhance endotoxemia severity, mortality, and inflammatory cytokine expression in vivo, independent of hypoglycemia, demonstrating time-dependent PA-induced trained immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C98 are supported by in vivo experiments (Figure 4A-E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing dose-dependent and time-dependent effects. The inclusion of shorter time controls (0, 3, 6 hr) and hypoglycemia measurements strengthens the conclusions. The serum PA levels achieved are physiologically relevant.

results.result: Mice pre-exposed to PA for 12 hr showed basal cytokine levels comparable to controls immediately prior to LPS challenge, indicating they were not in a primed state, suggesting PA induces trained immunity rather than priming.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 4F) showing no elevation in baseline cytokines. This is an important distinction between trained immunity and priming. However, the authors acknowledge they have not fully characterized the initial inflammatory response to PA, which is a limitation.

results.result: PA exposure followed by a 7-day rest period (PA→SC mice) still resulted in increased disease severity and mortality upon LPS challenge compared to vehicle controls, demonstrating that PA induces long-lived trained immunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 are supported by experiments showing persistent effects after a 7-day washout period (Figure 4G-H). This is critical evidence for long-lived trained immunity. However, the authors note the survival difference was not significant, suggesting PA may not be the sole driver of mortality in KD-fed mice.

results.result: PA pre-treatment (12 hr) enhanced clearance of Candida albicans infection in Rag1-/- mice, as evidenced by significantly reduced kidney fungal burden, demonstrating the beneficial aspect of PA-induced trained immunity in infection resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are supported by CFU quantification data (Figure 4I) in Rag1-/- mice lacking adaptive immunity. This demonstrates the dual nature of trained immunity (beneficial for infection, detrimental for inflammatory disease) and confirms lymphocyte-independent effects.

results.result: Co-treatment of BMDMs with oleic acid (OA) and PA significantly reduced PA-induced hyper-inflammatory responses to LPS, demonstrating that OA-dependent depletion of ceramides can reverse PA-mediated trained immunity in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C115 are supported by ELISA data (Figure 5A-C) showing OA blocks PA effects. This provides further mechanistic support for the ceramide pathway and demonstrates plasticity of the trained immunity phenotype. The experiment is well-controlled.

results.result: Systemic OA injection (300 mM i.p.) for 3 days prior to LPS challenge completely rescued KD-fed mice from enhanced hypothermia and mortality, demonstrating that OA can reverse SFA-induced trained immunity in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C121 are supported by in vivo experiments (Figure 5D-E) showing complete rescue of disease phenotype with OA treatment. This is a striking demonstration of the plasticity of dietary fatty acid effects and provides potential therapeutic implications. The result is well-supported.

results.result: The manuscript demonstrates that dietary saturated fatty acids, specifically palmitic acid, induce long-lived trained immunity through ceramide synthesis, resulting in enhanced inflammatory disease severity but also improved pathogen clearance, with plasticity demonstrated by oleic acid reversal.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C138 represent the overall conclusions synthesizing all major findings. The claims are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence including in vitro, in vivo, conventional, germ-free, and mechanistic studies. The work demonstrates novelty in showing SFA-induced trained immunity in wild-type mice and identifying the ceramide pathway.

results.result: The manuscript appropriately cites and contextualizes prior work on trained immunity, dietary fatty acids, ceramide metabolism, and clinical sepsis to support the rationale and interpretation of the current findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C111 (selected citations) represent background knowledge and prior work that is appropriately cited. The citations appear accurate and relevant to the claims made. The authors appropriately distinguish their novel findings from prior work, particularly the Christ et al. 2018 study in Ldlr-/- mice.
